content:
I am running a research project on how people perceive the similarity between everyday situations. I will first give you 24 short vignettes, each describing a situation (labeled V1 to V24). In later messages I will show you other texts and ask you to rate their similarity to these vignettes. For now, read the vignettes and reply only: "Ready."

V1: Zoe, 44, sells ceramics online. Another seller she knows only as MarekCeramics proposes a joint bulk order of clay and glaze: if Zoe wires him two hundred dollars, his wholesaler's minimum is met and both of them cut their material costs nearly in half for the year. They have never met, and the wholesaler ships everything to his address, with Zoe's share to be forwarded on. The savings would let both shops take on bigger commissions. Zoe hovers over the transfer button.

V2: Priya, 52, runs a fruit stall at the covered market. A supplier's delivery error leaves her with twice her usual stock of ripe peaches at no extra charge, more than she can possibly sell before they spoil. Two stalls down, Samir lost most of his produce that morning when his cooler failed, and he stands behind nearly empty tables. He hasn't asked for help. Priya looks at her overflowing crates and considers how many belong on his counter.

V3: Hana, 24, has finally saved three hundred dollars toward the transmission repair her car urgently needs; without the car she cannot get to her early shifts. Her brother Milo asks to borrow most of it for festival tickets that go on sale tonight, promising vaguely to pay her back sometime. The mechanic has quoted her a firm price and a Friday appointment. Hana looks at her savings envelope and decides how much of it she can afford to release.

V4: At an estate sale, Liam, 26, spots a sealed lot of vinyl records priced at ninety dollars, sold only as one lot. He has fifty on him. Sofia, a stranger flipping through the same crate, has the rest and knows the resale market well; between her contacts and his cash, the lot could bring back double what it costs. She proposes pooling their money on the spot, with her handling the sales. Liam fingers the bills and decides how much to put in.

V5: Owen, 55, receives a two-hundred-dollar gear voucher from his kayak club in recognition of volunteer hours spent repairing the boat shed. Nadia, another member, logged nearly as many hours on the same repairs, but the club's rules allowed only one award. She congratulated him warmly and asked for nothing. The voucher can be divided into smaller ones at the shop. Owen turns it over in his hands, weighing what Nadia's work entitles her to.

V6: Amara, 21, has spent the whole term building a meticulous set of exam notes, hundreds of hours of summaries and worked problems. Josh, a classmate, asks her to send him the full file. He has never shared anything of his own, and last year a study guide she lent him circulated through half the class within a week. The exam is graded on a curve. Amara hovers over the attachment, deciding how many pages, if any, to send.

V7: Naomi, 36, a freelance designer embedded with an agency, has fifteen unbilled hours left this month. Her colleague Pieter is assembling a pitch for a client whose account would roughly double the workload, and the income, for both of them next quarter. The pitch only stands a chance if Naomi puts her hours into the visuals now, unpaid, before the deadline. If it lands, they split the account. Naomi opens her calendar and decides how many hours to commit.

V8: Ingrid, 61, harvests an enormous crop of tomatoes and squash from her allotment, far more than she can eat or preserve. Her neighbor Harold, 79, lives alone on a small pension and has mentioned that fresh produce has become a luxury for him. He has never asked her for anything and cannot see over her fence. Loading crates into her wheelbarrow, Ingrid considers how many of them Harold's situation calls for her to set on his porch.

V9: Lucille, 63, owns a food truck and paid well above the usual rate to secure twenty kilos of flour during a regional shortage. Marco, who runs a crepe stand nearby, offers to buy half at cost, saying he is nearly out. Lucille's weekend bookings, two markets and a private event, will use every kilo she has, and missing them would cost her far more than the flour did. She looks at her stacked sacks and settles on her answer.

V10: Hugo, 50, owns a wood lathe; Anouk, a fellow hobbyist, has a barn stocked with seasoned walnut she cannot turn into anything. The autumn craft fairs are approaching. If Hugo hauls the lathe to her barn for the season, together they can produce and sell twice the bowls either could manage alone and split the proceeds. Moving it means his own workshop sits idle, and everything depends on Anouk putting in the sanding and finishing. Hugo eyes his trailer hitch and weighs the move.

V11: Marisol, 34, a project coordinator, receives a five-hundred-dollar spot bonus after her team's product launch. The award was issued in her name alone, but her colleague Deshawn stayed late for weeks preparing the data that made the launch possible, and he will receive nothing. The money is already in her account, and Deshawn has no way of knowing it exists. Marisol sits down to decide how much of the bonus, if any, she should pass along to him.

V12: Boris, 47, grabs the last two bags of quick-set concrete at the hardware store before a forecast downpour; his half-finished patio footing will be ruined if it isn't sealed today. In the parking lot, a stranger named Petra asks whether he would sell her one bag for her own weekend project. Boris did the math at the shelf: both bags are barely enough to finish before the rain. He weighs her offer against the job waiting at home.

V13: Aiko, 66, has raised sixty tomato seedlings in her small greenhouse, far more than her shaded yard can support. Her neighbor Stan has a large, sun-drenched plot but no head start on planting. If Aiko hands her trays over the fence, Stan will do the watering and staking, and they will divide a harvest much bigger than either could manage separately. Whether it works depends on Stan tending the plants through the summer. Aiko counts her trays and decides how many to pass across.

V14: Callum, 29, wins two hundred fifty dollars in an online essay contest. A forum member known only as quietfern spent hours giving him line-by-line feedback on his drafts, expecting nothing, and has no idea he even entered. The platform lets members send money to each other anonymously. Staring at the notification, Callum thinks about how much of the prize quietfern's help earned, and whether he should transfer a portion before he spends any of it on himself.

V15: Iris, 38, has paid one hundred forty dollars to rent a bass boat for the entire day, planning to scout every cove of the lake before next month's fishing tournament. At the dock, another angler, Ken, asks whether she would give up the afternoon half so he could take the boat out. Iris mapped her route around a full day on the water; the scouting is the whole point of the expense. She checks her watch and makes her decision.

V16: Wen, 28, a graduate student, holds thirty booked hours on the department's spectrometer this semester. Her classmate Dario has a freezer full of promising samples but no machine time. If Wen gives half her hours to running his samples, the combined dataset would support a joint paper far stronger than anything either could publish alone, with both their names on it. Dario would owe her the analysis work in return. Wen looks at the booking sheet and considers how many hours to sign over.

V17: Theo, 27, is handed four hundred dollars in cash by his grandmother at her birthday dinner, with a murmured wish that it 'help the grandchildren'. His cousin Lila, who visits their grandmother far more often than Theo does, was in the kitchen and received nothing. Nobody else knows about the gift, and Lila will never find out unless Theo tells her. Driving home, Theo weighs whether an even split, or something more, is what the moment calls for.

V18: Felix, 33, lists his camera for four hundred dollars on a resale site. A buyer with the handle shutterbay_ed pushes him to ship immediately, saying the payment will 'clear in a few days' and that waiting will kill the deal. Felix has read seller forums full of stories where the parcel went out and the money never arrived, with no way to recover either. The camera sits boxed on his desk while he decides whether it leaves his hands.

V19: Edith, 59, owns the bookshop next to Ravi's café. Cutting an archway between their premises would cost eight hundred dollars, so that coffee drinkers browse books and readers order coffee. Ravi can cover half but no more, and neither business alone would gain enough to justify the expense; combined, their projections show foot traffic rising for both within months. The work starts only if Edith puts in her share now. She studies the quote and picks up her phone.

V20: Yuki, 19, is awarded twenty hours of free tutoring credit as the top student in her chemistry section. Her classmate Bela finished with an identical average, but the credit went to Yuki on a tiebreak based on submission time. The tutoring office allows credit to be transferred between students, and Bela, who struggles to afford extra help, doesn't know transfers are possible. Yuki holds the voucher and wonders whether an even division is what the tie truly deserves.

V21: Greta, 58, stores forty liters of generator fuel for the storm season, bought at a premium after last year's outages. Her neighbor Bill knocks and asks to take half, saying he'll replace it once the roads reopen. Last winter he carried off two cans on the same promise and never brought anything back. Forecasters expect a week of severe weather. Greta stands at her shed door, calculating how much fuel she can part with and still cover herself.

V22: Jamal, 30, has four hundred dollars set aside. His friend Toby has built a smoker and secured a weekend spot at the food market, but he cannot afford brisket and packaging on his own. Toby's numbers suggest that with Jamal's money for stock, the stall could return roughly double what they put in, split between them. Neither could run it alone: Toby has the equipment and permit, Jamal the cash. Jamal reads the figures again and reaches for his wallet.

V23: At a street festival, Tomás, 45, wins ten meal vouchers in a random drawing at a food stall. The woman behind him in line, Renata, missed the prize by a single ticket and shrugs it off with a smile before turning away. Tomás has no plans to use more than a few vouchers before they expire tonight. He watches her walk toward the exit and asks himself how many vouchers it would be right to press into her hand.

V24: Devon, 41, keeps a personal reserve of eighty dollars for buying materials on site jobs. His coworker Rex asks him to front the money for supplies for tomorrow's shift, promising to square up on payday. Twice before, Rex has taken such advances and repaid nothing, brushing off every reminder. The company won't cover the loss. Devon counts the bills in his pocket and decides how much, if anything, he can hand over without leaving himself exposed again.
Ready.

TEXT A:

James was going through a rough financial patch. He struggled to make ends meet and had no savings
left. One morning, he received an unexpected email from a government welfare agency he had applied
to months ago. "Congratulations! You have been selected for financial assistance. You will be
receiving the full aid amount to help with your expenses."

As James went to the agency to collect, he found Mark, a neighbor. He learned that Mark also
applied but wasn't selected. Only James received the funds.

Now James faced a choice. Should he keep all the money for himself? James was tempted because he
really needed the money, and Mark was just an acquaintance. Or should he give some of it to Mark,
given that he was struggling? What should he do?

TASK 1. For each vignette V1-V24, rate on a 0-100 scale how similar the situation in TEXT A is to the situation in the vignette, considering the situation as a whole: what is at stake, the relationship between the parties, the setting, and the structure of the decision each party faces. 0 = the two situations have nothing in common; 100 = they are essentially the same situation.

TASK 2. Now imagine a person in the situation of TEXT A, asking themselves: "What kind of situation is this? What does it remind me of?" Distribute exactly 100 points across the 24 vignettes according to how strongly each would come to mind as a similar experience. You may give 0 points to any vignette.

OUTPUT FORMAT: return a single JSON object, no other text:
{"ratings": {"V1": <0-100>, ..., "V24": <0-100>}, "retrieval_points": {"V1": <int>, ..., "V24": <int>}}
The retrieval points must sum to exactly 100.

After weeks of intense preparation, Steve was thrilled to learn that his team was awarded a
performance bonus for exceeding their sales target. The recognition felt satisfying—a tangible
reward for the long hours he'd poured into work and the many nights he'd stayed late fine-tuning
his pitch. The director called Steve to discuss the bonus and said: "You guys did great. Since you
are the team leader, the full bonus is allocated to you. However, you may choose to give a portion
to your teammate Max if you wish. The final decision is yours."

Now Steve faced a choice. He could keep the full bonus, as initially allocated. Or he could give
some to Max, knowing that Max made a significant contribution to the team's success. What should
he do?

Consider again TEXT C. In that situation there is another party on the other side: the person who receives what is sent and decides how much to give back.

Here are four descriptions of possible counterparts:

R1: Ruben, 27, received funds from an online acquaintance to place a joint bulk order of trading cards, with the goods shipped to Ruben's address for splitting. When the boxes arrived, Ruben sold the entire lot, kept the acquaintance's portion of cards and cash alike, and quietly deleted the message thread.
R2: Marguerite, 48, took the five hundred dollars her friend advanced her to stock a weekend market stall. Sales went well, roughly doubling the stake. Once the tables were folded, Marguerite counted the takings and handed her friend back considerably more than half; his money had made the weekend possible, and she made sure his return reflected it.
